title: Awakening on the Way of the Bodhisattva
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva, the eighth-century text Kanho has carried for years, and reads from three of its sections. Kanho opens with the Han inscription, "Do not waste your life," then reads Shantideva's prayer on taking hold of bodhicitta and tells of imagining retirement and grabbing at a moment of spacious peace that vanished. The Patience chapter's warning about anger meets Kanho's own family history and the book tucked in Kanho's purse at City Hall. Kanho closes with a taste of the wisdom chapter and the story that Shantideva levitated until only his voice remained above the clouds.

sentences.text: Unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.
Good morning, my friends.
How are you?
I really appreciate that you took some time out of your Sunday to come and attend this.
I really do appreciate it.
And I really appreciate Desiree, who is the complete Doan Ryo and who keeps time for us, and Talus, who is our tech wizard in the background, who is recording and making all the digital stuff happen.
And also a big thank you to Judith, who is just modeling such nice form all the time.
So we all need to do it together, and also, they have been at it for a very long time.

So at the end today, I will ask if anybody is willing to learn the role of Doan Ryo, so Desiree is not on the spot all the time, and maybe if we have another tech wizard, if Talus needs relief, that would be great.
So whether this is your first time or whether this feels like coming home to old friends, let us bring our minds to the fact that this is a brand new moment.
No matter how old or young you are, let us appreciate this, that this moment has never before existed and will never come again.
This moment, and as soon as we mentioned it, the moment is already gone, replaced by the next moment, which usually looks a lot like the moment before.
And because of this, we believe that time is passing.
Today, I am asking you to appreciate this singularity, the rareness of this moment, just this.
We are called to meditation by the sound of the Han, a wooden board being struck by a mallet.
On the Han, it says,
*Great is the matter of birth and death.
Time passes swiftly.
Everything is lost.
Awake, awake.
Do not waste your life.*
And being aware of time passing us by, we can see that every moment offers choices, opportunities, a pivot point.
What will I do with this moment?
Where will I go?
Will it be living by vow?
Will it be numbing out in front of the computer?
Will it be chasing entertainment and pleasures?
I find these pandemic times very challenging.
It is easy to lose track and get lost in reading the latest whatever on Google, and suddenly the day is half over.
I am grateful for schedules and calendars that remind me of upcoming events, studies, and so on.
Lately, I've been really digging into Reb Anderson's book, *Being Upright*, which we will study during the upcoming precepts class.
And I've been loving Shantideva's *Way of the Bodhisattva* for a very long time.
And we actually will be starting to read that book this coming Thursday.
Here we go.
This coming Thursday.
Please feel free to join one or the other of these events if your time and energy allow for it.
If time and energy do not allow for it, just don't even waste another thought.
But back to the *Way of the Bodhisattva*.
Considering that there are so many books about Zen and Zen practice that are way more modern, why this one?
So a little bit about Shantideva.
He was an eighth-century Indian philosopher, Buddhist monk, poet, and scholar at the University of Nalanda.
He followed the Machamaka philosophy of Nagarjuna.
He is also today considered one of the eighty-four Mahasiddhas.
And I read this really great definition by Robert Thurman of Mahasiddhas.
He calls them Psychonaut's.
Psychonaut's.
I'm quoting Bob Thurman now.
*In parallel with our astronauts, the materialist science adventurers whom we admire for their courageous explorations of the outer space, which we consider the matrix of material reality.
The inverse astronauts, the Psychonaut's, voyage deep into inner space, encountering and conquering the angels and demons in the depths of their subconscious minds.*
I can tell you though that Shantideva's fellow students at Nalanda did absolutely not see him as a Sita or a Mahasiddha as a person who has achieved spiritual realization and supernatural power.
Quite the opposite was the fact.
Given the opportunity, Shantideva did rise to the challenge and gave the teaching of the *Way of the Bodhisattva*, the *Bodhicharyavatara*.
He shared this teaching of the awakened heart of Bodhicitta.
You may have encountered that word Bodhicitta in your studies before.
It is enlightenment mind, the mind that strives towards awakening, empathy, and compassion for the benefit of all sentient beings.
On the relative level, Bodhicitta is the yearning to free oneself from ignorance and old habit patterns for the benefit of the world.
For the benefit of all beings, the desire to end suffering, the beautiful aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all.
On the ultimate level, Bodhicitta is perfect compassion, the non-dual wisdom of emptiness, the essence of the awakened mind.
Gradually, throughout the *Way of the Bodhisattva*, Shantideva reveals the connection between the relative and the absolute, two aspects of the same realization.
The *Way of the Bodhisattva* leads us to the first tender sprouts of Bodhicitta in our hearts and minds.
Then it helps us to support and secure those sprouts so they can develop firmer roots and we don't lose what we have.
And the last chapters show us ways to grow and strengthen Bodhicitta in us.
And often when we hear lectures on the *Way of the Bodhisattva*, the teacher picks up one aspect of the teaching and expands on it.
And I tried something a little bit different by presenting all these three aspects of the first tender roots, strengthening, and then the growth in one talk.
So I will read three quotes from the book throughout the talk.
Now I want to talk about imagination a little bit.
When we imagine something, we, well maybe I shouldn't say we, I always miss important aspects.
Imagination gives us sensations and ideas in the mind without any immediate input provided through our senses.
It is forming out of the experiences in our minds.
Imagination can be anything: recreations of past experiences, vivid memories with imagined changes, or completely invented.
Before I retired, I would imagine myself doing all these fun things, traveling the world, having fantastic adventures.
I basically imagined everything as it was at the time, minus the eight to five work schedule.
My imagination so missed the boat.
I forgot that my body would be twenty or thirty years older, that my life might take a totally different direction.
I just figured that I'd be out kayaking or hiking all the time.
That home would be more like the place where I dry out my tent every once in a while.
My mind was looking for permanent road trip and had no idea that for twenty years, half my annual vacation would be spent in Seychelles or I would be at Tassajara or Green Gorge for a month.
No regrets though.
Now, I imagine that all my thoughts and ideas about awakening and enlightenment are just as flawed.
I realized that I don't even want to imagine.
My mind leads me astray all the time.
When I had started to practice a bit, my mind came up with all kinds of ideas.
I had these stories about Zen monks, and somehow I settled on this idea that if I got this Zen thing right, nothing could make me hurt anymore.
There would be no more pain.
And I landed on the idea that detachment was the key.
So I kept on working on it.
Detachment.
Detachment.
I just couldn't figure it out until one day, as I was driving home from work.
There it was: wide open, peaceful spaciousness that went on forever.
Everything right there and intimate, while at the same time about an arm's length away.
And fool that I am, what did I do?
I grabbed that feeling with both hands.
Oh yes, this feels nice.
I wanted to be like this all the time.
And bam, it was gone.
Yeah, so imagination.
But back to Shantideva.

Since the *Way of the Bodhisattva* is separated into three distinct segments, I will offer a few verses from each segment: the dawning of Bodhicitta, the maintaining, and the intensifying of Bodhicitta.
I will open by reading a passage that is also known sometimes as Shantideva's prayer.
*It is from the chapter taking hold of Bodhicitta, and it is pure and wonderful aspiration.
May I be a guard for those who are protectorless.
A guide for those who journey on the road.
For those who wish to cross the water, may I be a boat, a raft, a bridge.
May I be an aisle for those who yearn for land.
A lamp for those who yearn for light.
For all who need a resting place, a bed.
For those who need a servant, may I be their slave.
May I be the wishing jewel, the vase of wealth.
A word of power, and the supreme healing.
May I be the tree of miracles, for every being the abundant cow.
Just like the earth and space itself, and all the other mighty elements, for boundless multitudes of beings, may I always be the ground of life, the ground of varied sustenance.
Thus, for everything that lives, as far as are the limits of the sky, may I be constantly their source of livelihood, until they pass beyond all sorrow.

Just as the Buddhas of the past have brought forth the awakened mind, and in the presets of the Bodhisattvas, step by step abode and trained, likewise, for the benefit of beings, I will bring to birth the awakened mind, and in those presets, step by step, I will abide and train myself.*
Isn't that beautiful?
As you can tell, me thinking is not part of the awakening, of the dawning of Bodhicitta.
It is like the inscription of the Han: great is the matter of birth and death.
Time passes swiftly, everything is lost.
Awake, awake, do not waste your life.
Or as it is sometimes translated, do not spend your days and nights in vain.
It cuts right to the chase.
When I read these lines, I feel really challenged.
Can I meet these lofty goals?
Am I willing to put out?
Am I willing to live up to my Bodhisattva vows?
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
The next passage I will read is from the Patience chapter.
I believe the Patience chapter is the most widely read part of this book.
Interestingly, Pema Chodron in her commentary, *No Time to Lose*, renamed the chapter Working with Anger.
*All the good works gathered in a thousand ages, such as deeds of generosity and offerings to the blissful ones, a single flash of anger shatters them.
No evil is similar to anger, no austerity to be compared with patience.
Steep yourself therefore in patience, in various ways insistently.
Those tormented by the pain of anger have never known tranquility of mind.
Strangers will they be to everything, will neither sleep nor feel secure.
Even those dependent on their Lord, for gracious gifts of honor and of wealth, will rise against and slay a master who is filled with wrath and hate.
All these ills are brought about by wrath, our sorrow bearing enemy.
Those who seize and crush their anger down will find their joy in this and future lives.*
Getting what I do not want, and all that hinders my desire, in discontent my anger finds its fuel, from this it grows and beats me down.
Therefore, I will utterly destroy the sustenance of this my enemy, the foe who has no other purpose but to hurt and injure me.
So come what may, I'll not upset my cheerful happiness of mind.
Detection never brings me what I want,
my virtue will be warped and marred by it.
If there is a remedy when trouble strikes, what reason is there for detection?
If there is no help for it, what use in being glum?
Maybe you'll say, well, this guy exaggerates a lot.
But think about it.
Think about a long-held friendship that ends over a conflict.
Years and years of being friends can be destroyed just in one moment.
And even if we are able to smooth things out, if we are able to knot together that torn string, there's still a knot in it that we might bump against every once in a while.
Shantideva really goes into greater detail, but I had to stop someplace.
So of all my Dharma books,
The *Way of the Bodhisattva* has been my most constant companion over the years.
When I used to still work, when I took breaks or was going over to City Hall, this book would always be in my purse.
And I would pull it out and open it in a random spot and read a couple of verses.
And I was really good at having one eye on the road and the other one on the book.
Tim would really tease me when he would see me walking along, holding my book and reading, and he would wonder how often I stumble.
But this book, especially the Patience chapter, has given me a lot.
It caused me to investigate my attitude, especially towards people I did not like so much.
And it really made me look at my anger, because I came from a family where anger was cultivated and where it was very much related to the power structure inside the family.
So I did learn a lot from Shantideva.
We as Zen practitioners always emphasize Zazen as the entry to the awakened mind.
But at the same time, we should not disregard studying, learning, and gaining understanding.
Panna, a Pali word, means understanding, wisdom, and insight.
And it was described by the Buddha as another path of awakening.

And my experience with this book did show that these studies and exposing myself to Shantideva's view on anger and diligence, did heal some rifts inside me and smoothed some of my rougher edges, for sure.
There are several commentaries on the *Way of the Bodhisattva*, and most of them have one thing in common: they skipped the wisdom chapter.
Usually the writer says, the author says, oh, my book is already so long.
And so I will better write a completely different book, just dedicated to the wisdom chapter, because it is so great.
And then they don't write the book on the wisdom chapter.
Fortunately, the Dalai Lama did, and the title of it is *Practicing Wisdom*.
And if you may have it, it's this book.
And there's a new commentary out, which I have not, I'm not at the wisdom chapter yet.
And it's called *Bodhicharyavatara with commentary*.
So I'm just starting in on this.
Since I do not feel competent to give you any commentary on the wisdom chapter, I decided I will just start reading it and I'll give you a taste of what it says.
*All these branches of the doctrine, the enlightened sage, which is the Buddha, expounded for the sake of wisdom.
Therefore, they must cultivate this wisdom who have, who wish to have an end of suffering.
The relative and ultimate.
These, the two truths, are declared to be.
The ultimate is not within the reach of intellect.
For intellect is said to be the relative.
When ordinary folk perceive phenomena, they look on them as real and not illusory.
This, then, is the subject of debate, where ordinary people and yogis differ.
Forms and so forth, which we all perceive, exist by general acclaim, but not by valid reasoning.
They are false, just like, for instance, unclean things, regarded in the common view as pure.
But that he might instruct the worldly, our protector spoke of things.
But these, in truth, like even momentariness.
Now, if you say it's wrong to claim the momentary as the relative, there is no fault.
For momentariness is relative for yogis, but for worldly beings, ultimate.
Were it otherwise, the common view would fault the yogic insight into corporal impurity.*
I will end here.
Though I would not mind sitting down right here and to read the whole book together with you.
It is said that when Shantideva spoke the wisdom chapter, he levitated higher and higher.
So in the end, the only thing left was his voice coming down from above the clouds.
If you should ever pick up this book, also take a look at the two meditation practices that are explained in the appendix: equalizing self and other and exchanging self and other.
I find this practice very challenging when it is done with a strong intention and a sincere heart.
It is very painful and, like I said, pretty intense.
But I have talked too much already today.
And I hope that you have found something useful for your practice in Shantideva's words.
If not, please forget it all and continue with your own practice today and days to come.
I want to express my deepest gratitude to all the teachers who bring a little bit more light into this world.
I am deeply grateful to Shantideva to lay out yet another path to find support and grow our bodhicitta.
I am deeply grateful to the Dalai Lama who has taught the *Way of the Bodhisattva* over and over.
And to say about this book, if I have any understanding of compassion and the practice of the Bodhisattva path, it is entirely on the basis of this text that I possess it.
I am deeply grateful to my teacher, Soketsu Norman Fischer, who introduced me to Shantideva.
And I am deeply grateful to Norman Tim Burnett, who gives some space to my love of the *Bodhicharyavatara*.
And I'm deeply grateful to all of you for sharing this deep and brief exploration of bodhicitta.
May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.

But that he might instruct the worldly, our protector spoke of things. But these, in truth, like even momentariness. Now, if you say it's wrong to claim the momentary as the relative, there is no fault. For momentariness is relative for yogis, but for worldly beings, ultimate. Were it otherwise, the common view would fault the yogic insight into corporal impurity. I will end here. Though I would not mind sitting down right here and to read the whole book together with you.
